passages.happening:
‘On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar, the king’s command and edict were to be executed. On this day the enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them, but their plan was overturned and the Jews overpowered those who hated them’ (verse 1).

In every province the Jews gather in their cities against those who sought to harm them, and no one can stand against them (verse 2). The officials of the provinces help the Jews, out of fear of Mordecai, who has grown great in the palace (verses 3-4). In the citadel of Susa the Jews fight their enemies and kill the ten sons of Haman, ‘but they did not lay a hand on the plunder’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The thirteenth of Adar falls in the late winter of about 473 BC, eleven months after Haman's decree.

Verse 1 states the book's great theme in one word: overturned. Those who hoped to master the Jews were mastered by them. The same verb, haphakh, will describe sorrow turned to joy in verse 22.

The Jews act under the king's second decree, which allowed them to defend themselves on the day set for their destruction. The text says that they struck those who sought to harm them and those who hated them, not neutral neighbors. And three times the chapter says that they did not lay a hand on the plunder, though the decree allowed it. Many readers connect that with Saul, who took plunder from Amalek against God's command. This time the plunder is left alone.

The chapter reports the fighting briefly, and these notes do not dwell on it.
passages.later: Saul's failure stands behind the refusal of plunder: ‘Saul and his troops spared Agag, along with the best of the sheep and cattle’ (1 Samuel 15:9).
passages.asks: The day chosen for their destruction became the day they survived. Ask what day or season in your life you thought would be the end, and how you came through it. And ask what you would leave untouched, as the Jews left the plunder, to show what you were fighting for.

passages.t: A second day in Susa, and rest
passages.happening:
The king tells Esther what has happened in Susa and asks what more she wants. She asks that the Jews in Susa may have one more day ‘to carry out today’s edict’ (verse 13), and that the bodies of Haman's sons be hung up. The king commands it, and on the fourteenth the Jews in Susa gather again, ‘but they did not lay a hand on the plunder’ (verse 15).

In the provinces, the Jews also gather to defend themselves, and the book gives a large number of their enemies who were killed, ‘but they did not lay a hand on the plunder’ (verse 16).

On the fourteenth day they rest, ‘making it a day of feasting and joy’ (verse 17). In Susa, where the fighting lasted two days, they rest on the fifteenth. ‘This is why the rural Jews, who live in the villages, observe the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day of joy and feasting. It is a holiday for sending gifts to one another’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The chapter explains a difference that is still kept. Jews in the villages celebrated on the fourteenth of Adar, while in Susa, where the fighting went on a second day, the celebration fell on the fifteenth. Later Jewish practice kept both: most communities celebrate on the fourteenth, and cities walled in the time of Joshua, above all Jerusalem, on the fifteenth, which is called Shushan Purim after Susa.

The numbers the chapter gives are large, and the ancient versions do not agree on them. The Greek translation of Esther gives a smaller figure for the provinces than the Hebrew.

What the chapter dwells on is not the fighting but the rest: the day after, when people stopped, feasted and sent gifts to one another.
passages.later: Revelation remembers the same customs of a festival day, when people ‘will celebrate and send one another gifts’ (Revelation 11:10).
passages.hard:
How should a reader understand the killing in this chapter?

This is the book's hardest chapter for many readers, and it should be read as such. Several things are worth weighing. The Jews act under a royal decree permitting defense against those who would attack them on a day set for their destruction, and the text says that they struck those who sought to harm them and those who hated them, not neutral neighbors. They refuse to take plunder, which the narrator stresses three times, which suggests that they fought to survive and not for gain.

Esther's request for a second day in Susa is harder to explain. Some see it as ending a continuing threat in the capital; others see it as going too far. Some scholars read the book as a stylized story with large round numbers, not a precise count; others defend its history, noting that the ancient versions already give different figures. Christian readers have also noted that the Bible records many events without approving every detail. Faithful readers differ on how much the narrator approves, and these notes take no side.

Two things are not in doubt. The New Testament forbids personal vengeance: ‘Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath’ (Romans 12:19). And nothing in this chapter gives anyone today a warrant to harm anyone, or to take revenge on any people, for any cause.
passages.asks: After the fighting came rest, feasting and gifts. Ask what it would mean for you to stop and give thanks after a hard season, instead of moving straight on. And ask how you can answer harm done to you without taking revenge.

passages.happening:
‘Mordecai recorded these events and sent letters to all the Jews in all the provinces of King Xerxes, both near and far’ (verse 20), to establish a yearly celebration on the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar. These are to be remembered as the days when the Jews gained rest from their enemies, ‘and the month in which their sorrow turned to joy and their mourning into a holiday’ (verse 22): days ‘of feasting and joy, of sending gifts to one another and to the poor’ (verse 22).

The chapter tells the story again in brief: Haman cast the Pur, the lot, to destroy the Jews, and his scheme came back on his own head (verses 24-25). ‘Therefore these days are called Purim, from the word Pur’ (verse 26). The Jews bind themselves and their descendants, ‘and all who join them’ (verse 27), to keep the two days every year. ‘These days should be remembered and celebrated by every generation, family, province, and city’ (verse 28).

Esther, with Mordecai, writes with full authority to confirm the days of Purim, and ‘Esther’s decree confirmed these regulations about Purim, which were written into the record’ (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
Pur comes from an Akkadian word for a lot. Haman used it to choose the day for the Jews' destruction, trusting fate to give him a good day. The feast takes its name, Purim, the plural, from that lot: a reminder that the day chosen for destruction became the day of rescue.

Purim was not one of the feasts commanded in the law of Moses. The Jewish community itself established it and accepted it as binding, as this chapter describes. It is known outside the book by the second century BC, when the book of Second Maccabees calls the fourteenth of Adar Mordecai's day.

The customs named in verse 22 are still at the heart of the feast: feasting and joy, sending portions of food to one another, and gifts to the poor. The reading of the whole scroll of Esther in the synagogue, with noise to drown out Haman's name, developed later in Jewish tradition. Remembering, in the Bible, is active. It means telling and celebrating what has been done so that each new generation knows it was kept.

Notice also all who join them in verse 27. The feast was for the Jewish people and for those who joined them.
passages.later: The law of Moses set the other feasts, and Purim stands beside them as a feast the people themselves established. Its spirit is the spirit of Psalm 30: ‘You turned my mourning into dancing’ (Psalm 30:11).
passages.hard:
Can a feast that the law of Moses did not command be holy?

Purim is a feast that the people themselves established, without a command in the law of Moses. Esther and Mordecai write letters, and the community accepts the days as binding for every generation.

Jewish tradition received Purim and kept it, and the scroll of Esther is read at it to this day. The book presents the feast as a right response to a real rescue: remembering, giving thanks, and caring for the poor. It does not claim to add to the law of Moses. It records how a scattered people chose to remember that they had been kept safe.
passages.asks: Purim joins feasting with gifts to the poor. Ask how you remember the times you were rescued, and whether your remembering includes those who have nothing. And ask what you will tell the next generation about how God kept you.
